However, fraught negotiations resulted in the blockage of several key proposals, including sanctions on fish imports, liquefied natural gas (LNG) transportation, and stricter entry requirements for Russian citizens. France and Italy notably opposed an entry ban for individuals who have fought for Russia against Ukraine, citing Schengen regulations, though analysts suggest the move was driven by a desire to protect tourism revenues. by Eurotopics | July 26, 2026, 9:51 am Flip Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied A tugboat guides the Russian oil tanker Anatoly Kolodkin as it arrives at the oil terminal in the port of Matanzas, northwestern Cuba, on March 31, 2026. Photo by Yamil LAGE / AFP Content Share Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Bluesky Email Copy Copied Flip After fraught negotiations, the EU Commission has decided on its 21st sanctions package against Russia. Restrictions on the Russian financial sector will be further tightened and the “price cap” on crude oil exports will remain at a low of $44 per barrel. But individual countries intervened to block numerous proposals to sanction fish imports, LNG transportation and entry requirements for tourists, for example. Sick of making sacrifices The protracted negotiations are a cause for concern for die Zeit (Germany): JOIN US ON TELEGRAM Follow our coverage of the war on the @Kyivpost_official . “That competing national interests play a role in the drafting of sanctions is in itself nothing new. ... Weeks of wrangling over concessions have left EU member states divided and flattened by sanction fatigue. The image they present will certainly appeal to Putin: that of a Europe which, five years into this war, is primarily focused on the individual interests of its member states. ... This is all the more tragic given that this package of sanctions could well be the last. For where else can measures be found that inflict sufficient damage on Russia without being too painful for Europe? The willingness of European governments to impose sanctions seems to be exhausted.” Advertisement No more hiding behind Orbán’s veto The haggling has been fierce, Latvia’s TVNet comments: “After four years of war and 20 rounds of sanctions, it is no longer possible to impose new restrictions without them also impacting major European companies and entire economic sectors. Consequently the sanctions policy is increasingly becoming a deal between member states – with each state only prepared to shore up the joint pressure on Russia if it can also protect its most sensitive interests. Viktor Orbán’s resignation has not resolved this contradiction. It has merely deprived other capitals of the opportunity to hide behind Budapest’s veto, forcing them to reveal far more clearly what each of them is unwilling to sacrifice in the name of sanctions.” Advertisement Other Topics of Interest Russia Cuts Funding for Putin’s Flagship Technology Projects Russia has reduced funding for several of Vladimir Putin’s flagship technology development projects in 2025 as the government redirects resources to sustain record military spending. Tourism should not suffer more The proposed entry ban on anyone who has fought for Russia against Ukraine was not included in this package. European Pravda (Ukraine) explains why: “France, Italy and – less openly – a string of other coastal states have flatly refused to address the issue as part of the package of sanctions against Russia – on the grounds that it would have to be implemented by changing Schengen regulations. But their real motive had little to do with legal concerns and was more about delaying a decision that would further impede the influx of Russian tourists, which has already been declining since the start of the large-scale invasion of Ukraine.” See the original version of this article here . https://www.mirror.co.uk/news/uk-news/br.text: British troops will join their German and French counterparts for a major Ukraine wargame as the Coalition of the Willing doubles down its support for the nation - while Donald Trump continues to sidle up to Vladimir Putin . Defence Secretary Wes Streeting announced this weekend that troops would make up a considerable force of 1,500 descending on Poland for the "major exercise" this November. He said while announcing the move in Washington DC, in the US, that servicemembers would be preparing to "prevail against Putin's aggression". But it will come without US involvement, as Trump breaks the country's relationship with Ukraine and tries to broker a new relationship with Russia . Speaking in Washington DC, Streeting said: “Ukraine is the front line for freedom everywhere, and it’s absolutely vital that they prevail against Putin’s aggression. We’re planning for the peace and freedom we want to see through our leadership of the coalition of the willing. “Next month thousands of personnel will take part in a major exercise in Poland to ensure we are ready to support the military training and post-war rebuilding that Ukraine will need.” The exercise is aimed at ensuring Nato forces are ready to provide Ukraine with security guarantees once the war is over, but will be done without the pact's largest member. Trump has placed himself at loggerheads with the UK and other allies over the conflict by refusing to say President Putin sparked the Ukraine war. When asked whether he had forgotten that it was the Russian leader who started the war, he did not respond directly and implied it was not straightforward. He said: “I know the details, OK, and at some point I’ll release the details.” Trump added: “But I don’t care anything except for one. I want that war ended.” Trump also denied the US was responsible for the disruption to Kyiv’s access to the vital Starlink satellite communications system, leaving the country exposed to attack. He made the comments after leaving the White House for a campaign rally in Georgia, came after he again rounded on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky . He said he was “not a big fan” and claiming he was “more difficult to deal with than Putin”, and early on Saturday signed an executive order which put a hold on a new sanctions package targeting the Russian economy. The president said the pause was in the national interest of the US.
